property_summary: For any caller and any timestamp, if fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether the reference contract always accepts the call (does not revert) and updates pastBlockTime; the mutant requiring 1 ether will accept calls with 1 ether and therefore there exist inputs (e.g. calls with 10 ether) where the mutant reverts while the reference accepts — so the invariant: calls with msg.value == 10 ether never revert on the reference but may revert on the mutant.

For any caller and any timestamp, a call to C.fallback with msg.value == 10 ether always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference implementation, while the mutant that requires 1 ether will cause such a call to revert for some inputs (e.g. when msg.value == 10 ether).

For any caller and any timestamp, a fallback call sending exactly 1 ether to the correct contract always reverts (since it requires 10 ether) while the mutated contract (which requires 1 ether) may accept such a call; i.e., calls with msg.value == 1 ether always revert on the reference but can succeed on the mutant.

For any caller and timestamp, calling C.fallback with msg.value equal to 10 ether never reverts on the reference contract (so the call succeeds), whereas the mutant that changed the required value to 1 ether will revert for at least some inputs when called with 10 ether, so the property is: 'a call to fallback sending 10 ether always succeeds on the reference'.

For any caller and any block timestamp, calling C.fallback with msg.value == 10 ether does not revert (succeeds) on the correct contract, while the mutant that changed the required value to 1 ether will sometimes revert for such calls (so the reference always accepts 10 ether but the mutant may reject it).

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract C always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp strictly increasing (so a second call in the same block will revert), whereas the mutant allowing >= permits a second call in the same block to succeed and thus violates the strict-increase rule.

For every valid fallback call sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract strictly increases pastBlockTime (each successful call must set pastBlockTime to a value strictly greater than its previous value); the mutant using >= allows a second call in the same block to succeed and thus can make pastBlockTime unchanged, violating strict increase.

For any successful fallback call sending exactly 10 ether, the contract's public pastBlockTime strictly increases (each call sets pastBlockTime to a value > its previous value); the mutant that uses >= can allow two successful calls in the same block leaving pastBlockTime unchanged and thus violates strict increase.

After any successful payable fallback call sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always records pastBlockTime equal to the current block timestamp (monotonic update), while the mutant may set pastBlockTime to block.number and thus not equal block.timestamp for some inputs.

For any caller and any timestamp/block state, after a successful payable fallback call sending exactly 10 ether the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp, whereas the mutant sometimes sets pastBlockTime to block.number so the getter pastBlockTime() will differ from block.timestamp (violating equality) for some fuzzed inputs.

For any successful payable call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always records pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp (the current block timestamp) after the call; the mutant that assigns pastBlockTime = block.number will sometimes leave pastBlockTime != block.timestamp, so asserting equality with block.timestamp distinguishes them.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any sender at any strictly-increasing timestamp, the reference contract only pays out the entire contract balance when block.number % 15 == 0, so address(c).balance remains > 0 for calls where block.number % 15 != 0; the mutant inverts this and will instead drain the contract when block.number % 15 != 0, violating that rule for some block numbers.

For any caller and any ether amount sent to fallback, the reference contract C only accepts calls that send exactly 10 ether (so its state variable pastBlockTime only updates when msg.value == 10 ether), whereas the mutant removes that restriction and will update pastBlockTime for other amounts — thus the general rule: after calling fallback with any amount != 10 ether, C.pastBlockTime remains unchanged, but the mutant may change it.

For any call to fallback with any ether amount, contract C only updates pastBlockTime when exactly 10 ether is sent; the mutant (which removed that require) may update pastBlockTime for other amounts, so the property: after calling fallback with any amount != 10 ether, C.pastBlockTime does not change (the mutant breaks this).

For any caller and any block where the fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether and a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract never sends any ether to the caller unless block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance remains unchanged except when block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant may transfer a small amount unconditionally and thus can reduce the contract balance for some inputs.

After any successful fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether and where block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp before any possible transfer (so c.pastBlockTime() == block.timestamp), whereas the mutant that moves the update after a conditional transfer can allow pastBlockTime to remain old when the transfer succeeds (e.g., when block.number % 15 == 0 and transfer to the caller succeeds).

For any caller and any admissible timestamp/eth/chain state where msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > c.pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp by the end of the fallback call; the mutant that moves that assignment after a conditional transfer can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when the conditional transfer succeeds, so the property is violated for some inputs (when block.number % 15 == 0 and the transfer to the caller succeeds).

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp by the end of the call; the mutant that moves the update after the conditional transfer can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when the transfer to the caller succeeds (e.g., when block.number % 15 == 0 and the recipient accepts funds), so there exist inputs (caller that accepts transfer and a block number divisible by 15) where the mutant violates this invariant.

For every admissible call where msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > c.pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the call's block.timestamp by the end of the call; the mutant that moves the update after a conditional transfer can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when the transfer to the caller succeeds (e.g. when block.number % 15 == 0 and the recipient accepts funds).

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > c.pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp by the end of the call; the mutant that moves that update after the conditional transfer can fail to update pastBlockTime when the conditional transfer executes successfully (e.g., when block.number % 15 == 0 and the recipient accepts ETH).
